passage:
Class teacher's note, 10C, end of term

Ramesh has run the waste-segregation drive in our block since August. Every morning he checks the three bins and puts up a chart. It has not been easy for him.

On Monday, in front of the class, Anand said, "What's the point? The garbage truck mixes it all anyway. You're wasting everyone's time." A few boys laughed. I saw Ramesh's jaw tighten.

He waited a moment. Then he said, "The truck used to mix it. Since October the municipality sends a separate van for dry waste. Our block sent two hundred kilos to recycling last month. It's small. But it's real." Anand shrugged. "Still won't save the planet." Ramesh said, "No. It'll make our block cleaner, though."

Afterwards he told me he felt like giving up. We talked about how change is slow and that he had chosen a place where he could make a real difference. He decided to keep going and to invite Anand to help weigh the bags next week. Anand, to my surprise, said yes.

qa.q: How many kilos did the block send to recycling last month?
qa.a: The block sent two hundred kilos to recycling last month.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's tightening jaw suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Ramesh felt hurt and angry when Anand called the drive pointless in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do well when Anand challenged him?
qa.a: Ramesh answered with calm facts about the separate van and the recycling total, and admitted the change was small but real.

qa.q: Why might Anand have agreed to help weigh the bags?
qa.a: Anand may have been more curious than he let on, and Ramesh's patient answer made the invitation feel sincere, not like a trap.

grounding: It shows a teen whose activism is called pointless by peers, answering with facts and patience, accepting that change is slow and acting where he can make a difference.

passage:
Thursday

Kishore said it again at lunch. "Afreen, your ramp campaign is useless. The management will never build it. Why bother?"

I wanted to throw my water bottle at him. Instead I counted to five and said, "Okay, here's why." I told him about Raghu in 8B, who uses a wheelchair and has to be carried up the six steps to the library every day by two peons. I told him the building rules say new schools must have ramps, and old ones are supposed to add them.

He said, "Rules mean nothing here."

I said, "Maybe. But the principal agreed to meet our group next Tuesday. That's more than nothing."

He didn't answer.

I know it might take a year. Maybe more. I'm trying to accept that. But I'm not trying to fix the whole country. I'm trying to fix six steps.

Raghu said thank you today, just for trying. That's enough for this week.

Afreen

qa.a: Six steps lead up to the library.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when Kishore called the campaign useless?
qa.a: Afreen felt angry and frustrated enough to want to throw a water bottle at him.

qa.q: Why is Afreen's focus on six steps a wise choice?
qa.a: It picks a real change Afreen can influence, which keeps the campaign going even though larger change is slow.

qa.q: How might Raghu feel about the campaign?
qa.a: Raghu seems grateful and touched, since he thanked Afreen just for trying, even before any ramp is built.

passage:
Monday night

I spent two hours watching that travel girl's videos again. Maldives, then Paris, then some hotel with a pool on the roof. Her hair is perfect in every clip. Then I looked around my room: the fan that wobbles, the wall with the damp patch, the same school bag since Class 8. My life felt so boring I wanted to cry.

Neelam didi came in and saw my face. She scrolled through with me and pointed at the tiny words: "paid partnership," "hosted by," "ad." "She's being paid to be there, Aditi. And she probably filmed that walk ten times."

I hadn't even noticed.

Then didi asked, "What do you actually like about her videos?" And I realised it's the camera work. The way she shoots from low angles and uses light.

So I've decided: I'll watch her for the filming, not the hotels. Tomorrow I'm going to try shooting our lane at sunset with Papa's old phone. The damp patch can stay out of frame.

qa.a: She pointed to "paid partnership," "hosted by" and "ad."

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling after two hours of watching the travel videos?
qa.a: Aditi felt envious and low, as if Aditi's own life was so dull it was worth crying over.

qa.a: Aditi decided to learn from the camera work rather than compare lifestyles, which turns envy into a skill to practise.

In Karaikudi, when the news broke that the singer was leaving the band, Sharmila was sitting outside her aunt's sari shop. She read the headline three times and burst into tears right there on the step.

She had listened to his songs every night since Class 7. She told him things in her diary. When he sang about being lonely at school, she felt he'd seen inside her.

Gargi found her still crying at the shop. "Sharmi? What happened?"

"He's leaving. It feels like someone died."

Gargi sat beside her. She didn't laugh. "You really love his music."

"It feels like he knows me," Sharmila said, and then heard how it sounded. He didn't know her. He didn't know her name, or her maths marks, or that her father worked in Dubai.

Gargi knew all of that.

"Want to come to the temple fair tonight?" Gargi asked. "We can put his songs on the way."

Sharmila wiped her face. "Okay."

qa.q: Where was Sharmila sitting when the news broke?
qa.a: Sharmila was sitting outside her aunt's sari shop.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she read the headline?
qa.a: Sharmila felt grief and shock, crying as though someone had died, because the singer felt close to her.

qa.q: What helped Sharmila keep her real friendship alive?
qa.a: Sharmila accepted Gargi's invitation to the temple fair, spending time with a friend who truly knows her while still enjoying the songs.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Sharmila's sadness?
qa.a: Gargi takes it seriously and does not laugh, understanding how much the music means to Sharmila.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels close to a star as though he knows her and cries at his news, enjoying the comfort while remembering he does not know her and keeping a real friendship alive.

For two years, Marek had watched the streamer every evening in his bedroom in Kraków. The man said "Hey, chat!" at the start of every stream and read out usernames, and once he'd read out Marek's. Marek had felt it all week.

On Sunday the streamer announced he was quitting for good. Marek sat in front of the screen with tears running down his face. He felt stupid, crying over someone he'd never met. But it felt like losing a friend.

He didn't reply to Freya's messages that night.

On Tuesday, Freya caught him at the school gate. "You've been ignoring me for two days. Did something happen?"

He almost said nothing. Then, "The streamer I watch quit. I know it's dumb."

"It's not dumb," Freya said. "You've watched him every day." She paused. "But he never knew you were sad. I did."

That landed. Marek said yes to board game night at Freya's on Friday. He still watched old clips sometimes. But he went.

When my craft videos started getting thousands of views last year, I was fifteen and didn't know what to do with the messages. I'm Rekha, by the way. Most were sweet: "love your paper flowers," "made this with my sister."

Then there was Rashmi. She wrote every single day. "Good morning Rekha di!" "You're my best friend, you're the only one who gets me." "I told you about my exam, why didn't you reply?" She was twelve.

At first it made me feel warm and important. Then it made me uneasy. I wasn't her best friend. I didn't know her.

I talked to my mother. Together we wrote a reply: "Thank you so much for watching, Rashmi, it means a lot. I read your messages when I can, but I can't reply to everyone. I hope you share your crafts with your friends at school and your family too. They're lucky to have you."

It felt cold to send. But I think being kind and honest together is the only fair thing.

qa.q: How old was Rashmi?
qa.a: Rashmi was twelve.

qa.q: What did Rekha feel when Rashmi's daily messages kept coming?
qa.a: Rekha felt warm and important at first, then uneasy, because Rashmi was treating Rekha as a best friend without really knowing Rekha.

qa.q: Why was Rekha's reply a wise one?
qa.a: The reply thanked Rashmi warmly but set a clear limit and pointed her to friends and family, which avoids feeding her dependence.

qa.q: How might Rashmi feel reading the reply?
qa.a: Rashmi might feel a little disappointed at first, but also appreciated, since Rekha thanked her and called her friends lucky.

grounding: It shows a teen with a public following who receives messages from a fan acting as a best friend, and answers with kindness and clear boundaries rather than feeding dependency.

passage:
Music teacher's note, re: Mohit, Class 10

Since Mohit reached the finals of the television singing show, he has received many letters. One fan, Ganga, has written nearly every week since June. I have read some with Mohit and his parents' permission. She writes as though they are best friends: about her school, her fights at home, her dreams. Last week she asked for his personal phone number and wrote, "You're the only one who understands me."

Mohit brought the letter to me looking worried. "I don't want to hurt her. But I don't know her. What if she's really lonely?"

We agreed on a reply together. He thanked her sincerely for her support and said her letters made him happy. He said he could not share his number or write often, and hoped she had people nearby she could talk to, maybe a teacher or her family. He signed a photo for her.

I have also suggested his parents forward the address to the show's fan-care team, in case she needs support.

qa.q: What did Ganga ask for in her last letter?
qa.a: She asked for his personal phone number.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he brought the letter?
qa.a: Mohit felt worried and torn, not wanting to hurt Ganga but knowing he did not really know her.

qa.q: How did Mohit's reply keep both kindness and boundaries?
qa.a: Mohit thanked her warmly and signed a photo, but did not share his number and gently suggested she talk to a teacher or her family.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel when she gets Mohit's reply?
qa.a: Ganga may feel a little let down about the number, but also warmly noticed, since he thanked her sincerely and sent a signed photo.

grounding: It shows a teen public figure receiving letters from a fan who writes as a best friend, answering with kindness and boundaries so as not to feed dependency.

Then at a concert, which I watched on a livestream, he mocked a girl in the front row for crying. Called her "drama queen" into the mic. Everyone laughed. A clip of it went everywhere.

Amandeep, you think these online fan fights are new? Let your Reena Masi tell you about 1998.

We had a fan club at school for one film hero, and there was another club for his rival. We made posters, wrote slogans on each other's desks. It felt wonderful, like having a family.

Then it turned nasty. There was a girl, Poonam, the only one in our class who liked the rival hero. We started leaving notes in her bag. Mean things about her looks. I wrote one too. Everyone laughed, and I felt so included.

One day I found her crying in the girls' toilet, the note in her hand. My handwriting. I'll never forget her face.

I left the club that week. I went to her and said sorry. She didn't forgive me for a long time, and she didn't have to.

So when your group starts roasting someone, Amandeep, remember: it feels like belonging. But a real person is holding that note.

qa.a: Reena felt included and happy to belong, which made the cruelty feel acceptable at the time.

qa.a: Finding Poonam crying with Reena's own note was the turning point, because it showed the real hurt behind the group fun and led her to leave and apologise.

qa.a: Poonam was probably lonely and frightened, targeted by notes about her looks and ending up crying alone.

It was exam week, and Simran had almost no pocket money left. But the video made it sound so simple.

The creator, who had helped her with physics for a year through free videos, was launching a "Topper Guarantee" course. "Only 5,999 today! Rank guaranteed or your money back!" A timer counted down. Forty-seven minutes.

Simran knew her mother's card was saved on the laptop. Her fingers hovered.

Her elder sister Seema walked in with two cups of tea. "What's that?" Simran explained, fast.

Seema read the page slowly. "Guaranteed rank? Nobody can guarantee that. And look at the refund terms." They were tiny: refund only if you "complete all modules and attend all live sessions," which was impossible during exams.

"But he's been so helpful," Simran said. "I trust him."

"That's what he's selling," Seema said gently. "Your trust. And it's Mummy's money, not yours."

Simran closed the laptop. The timer was still running. She let it.

qa.q: How long was left on the countdown timer?
qa.a: Forty-seven minutes were left on the timer.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling as her fingers hovered over the card?
qa.a: Simran felt tempted and pressured, trusting the creator and anxious about exams.

qa.q: What did Seema help Simran notice?
qa.a: Seema pointed out that no one can guarantee a rank, the refund terms were nearly impossible, and the money belonged to their mother.

qa.q: How might their mother have felt if the card had been used?
qa.a: Their mother would likely have felt upset and worried, both about the money and about how easily trust had been used to sell to Simran.

grounding: It shows a teen targeted by a creator who sells an expensive course to young fans, recognising that trust built online can be sold, checking claims and not spending money that is not hers.

In the back of the school bus in Thane, Chetan held out his phone to Eshaan. "Look at this. That gaming creator we watch. He says this app doubled his money in a day. You just predict match results."

Eshaan watched. The creator was laughing, a pile of notes on his desk. At the bottom, in small letters: "promotional content."

"It's betting," Eshaan said. "He's getting paid to show that."

Chetan went quiet. Then, "I already tried. I put in the money Papa gave me for the tuition fee. I lost it. Two thousand." His voice cracked. "I thought I'd win it back. Now it's all gone, and I'm scared to tell him."

Eshaan felt his own chest go tight. "You have to tell someone today. I'll come with you."

After school they went to Chetan's flat. Chetan's father listened, very serious, then put his hand on his son's shoulder. "I'm glad you told me. We'll delete this app together tonight and talk to your tuition sir about the fee."

The rally ground was packed, the loudspeakers crackling, and it had started to drizzle. Madhuri, pressed between strangers, couldn't hear her friend Kavitha half the time. But she heard the leader.

He spoke about young people building a new city, about dignity, about jobs for everyone. The crowd roared. Madhuri felt goosebumps down her arms. She was shouting along before she knew it.

On the crowded bus home, soaked, she was still glowing. "Wasn't he amazing?"

Kavitha, wringing out her dupatta, said, "He was. What has he actually done, though? He's been in the council for five years."

Madhuri didn't know.

That night, with the power flickering, they looked up his council record on Kavitha's phone. Two promised flyovers, one finished. A school road still broken. A contract for his brother-in-law's firm.

Madhuri was quiet. "The speech was still good."

"It was," Kavitha said. "Now we know what to ask him next time."

The young councillor who spoke at the school's annual day was the best speaker Ojas had ever heard. She talked about clean parks, safe streets, libraries for every ward. The whole auditorium stood up and clapped. Ojas's heart was racing.

At home in their Jayanagar flat, he told his cousin Vijay, "I want to work for her when I'm older."

Vijay, who was in college, didn't laugh. "Okay. What has she done so far?"

"She said she'd build libraries."

"Did she?"

Ojas didn't know. So they checked the ward website together. One library had been opened, in fact. Two parks had been cleaned. But the "safe streets" plan was only on paper, and the contract for the park lights had gone to a firm that had also donated to her campaign.

Ojas frowned. "So is she good or bad?"

"Maybe both. That's what you check," Vijay said. "Enjoy the speech. Then read the record."

Ojas wrote her name in his notebook, with three questions under it.

qa.q: Where did the councillor speak?

passage:
Friday. Farida lay on her bed scrolling. A girl from class was in Goa. Three girls from tuition were at a birthday party she hadn't been invited to, all matching outfits. Someone had a new haircut that looked perfect. Two hours passed. She felt heavy and left out, and her own weekend of homework and a cousin's visit looked tiny.

Sunday. Her older cousin, visiting, noticed her face. "Scroll time?" Farida nodded. Her cousin laughed. "You know that Goa girl probably posted her best photo out of fifty, right? Nobody posts the mosquito bites." Farida smiled despite herself. She set a timer: thirty minutes a day on the app, no more.

Wednesday. After the timer rang, Farida felt the old itch to keep scrolling. Instead she messaged Anjali: "Chai at the corner stall after tuition?" Anjali replied in a second: "YES. I've had the worst week." They sat at the stall for an hour, talking about nothing, and laughing so hard the chai went cold. Nobody took a photo.

qa.q: How long did Farida set the timer for each day?
qa.a: Farida set the timer for thirty minutes a day.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling after two hours of scrolling on Friday?
qa.a: Farida felt heavy and left out, as if her own weekend was small next to everyone else's posts.

qa.q: What did Farida do on Wednesday instead of scrolling, and why did it help?
qa.a: Farida messaged Anjali for chai, which gave her real company and laughter instead of more comparison.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Farida's message arrives?
qa.a: Anjali seems relieved and happy, since she replied at once and said she had had the worst week.

grounding: It shows a teen who sees friends' holidays and parties online and feels left out, then remembers they post highlights, limits scrolling and messages a friend instead.

passage:
Vaibhav, you've been on that phone all evening looking at other people's holidays. Come here. Your Sabina Phuppo also went through this, you know. Not with phones then, with the early photo sites, but same thing.

I was sixteen. Every weekend my classmates uploaded albums: beach trips, farmhouse parties, new dresses. I sat in our two-room flat in Bhopal refreshing the page and feeling like I lived in a cupboard. I stopped enjoying anything I actually did.

One day my best friend Nargis told me, "Sabina, I uploaded thirty photos of my cousin's wedding. You know what I didn't upload? The fight my parents had in the car." That shocked me. Her photos had looked so happy.

After that I made a rule: the computer only for half an hour after homework. And when I felt that sinking feeling, I'd walk to Nargis's house instead.

That's all I'm saying. You're seeing their best moments, beta. Put it down, and go call your friend.

qa.q: Where did young Sabina live?
qa.a: She lived in a two-room flat in Bhopal.

qa.q: What was young Sabina feeling while refreshing her classmates' albums?
qa.a: Sabina felt left out and small, as if she lived in a cupboard, and stopped enjoying her own life.

qa.q: What changed Sabina's view, and what did she do next?
qa.a: Nargis revealing the fight she didn't post changed her view, and Sabina then limited computer time and visited Nargis instead of scrolling.

qa.q: What was it like for Nargis to post happy wedding photos after a family fight?
qa.a: Nargis may have felt a gap between how happy the photos looked and how tense the day really was.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling feeling left out by classmates' posted highlights, learning they were only highlights, limiting screen time and visiting a friend instead.
